<reason>Both sides fought a genuinely narrow, well-focused clash, but PRO controlled the decision rule. PRO correctly located the motion's operative words ("permit ... even if unit prices remain high") and forced CON to defend the residual case: a ministry offered a guarantee by one of a handful of fragile developers who will not accept a price ceiling. CON, to its credit, bit the bullet honestly ("yes, walk away"), but that answer became PRO's cleanest voter, and CON's justifications for it — that AMC terms are set ex ante and refusal doesn't ban emergency purchase, and that "PRO assumes the last developer disappears" — never squarely rebutted the leverage asymmetry PRO built in [A2.3]-[A2.4]. CON's strongest move was the structural distinction between a large fixed reward and a high marginal price, plus the sharp catch in [B4.5] that PRO oscillated between "paid whether the drug sits on the shelf" and "marginal sales are rounding error." But PRO's symmetric reply in [A4.2] ("if total revenue is equivalent, permitting the high-unit-price version costs nothing — so why forbid it?") blunted that, and PRO also neutralized CON's best emotional material: the squeezed-hospital-budget harm in [B1.6] is precisely what central availability payment abolishes, forcing CON to retreat to a more abstract "country's budget constraint" and "affordable expansion when needs grow." Against PRO's counterfactual (colistin, ICU, small budget line for a reserve drug) that retreat looked thinner. PRO's regret framing (one error fiscal, one fatal) was met only with the generic "budgets are not detached from patients." PRO incurred a real execution cost with two clipped turns, and CON's Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 discipline was clean, which keeps the margin from widening.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 forcing CON to state whether the ministry should walk away, and PRO's use of CON's "yes, walk away" in closing — combined with PRO's earlier turn of CON's hospital-affordability harm ([B1.6]) into an argument for central availability payments, which pushed CON off its most concrete access example.</best_rebuttal>
